posts.title: Multi-Tenant Integration Architecture: How to Build SaaS Integrations That Scale
posts.description: Building integrations into a multi-tenant SaaS product requires credential isolation, per-user routing, and a connection lifecycle that scales with your user base. This guide covers the architecture patterns that keep one tenant's data separate from another's, using viaSocket's Integration Layer as the implementation reference.
posts.author: Abhijeet Singh
posts.html:
Adding integrations to a multi-tenant SaaS product is not the same as adding integrations to a single-user tool. When thousands of tenants each connect their own Slack, HubSpot, or Stripe account, the architecture has to guarantee that one tenant's credentials and data can never reach another tenant's session — at any layer.

This guide covers the core architectural patterns for multi-tenant integrations: credential isolation, per-user connection routing, connection lifecycle management, and scaling considerations. The implementation examples use viaSocket's Integration Layer, which handles OAuth and token storage across 2,300+ apps.

The Multi-Tenant Integration Problem

A single-tenant integration is straightforward: one set of credentials, one OAuth token, one API client. A multi-tenant integration multiplies every concern:

  • Credential isolation: Each tenant's OAuth tokens must be stored and retrieved independently. A lookup error that returns the wrong tenant's token is a data breach.
  • Connection state: Each tenant has their own set of connected apps, which can be connected, disconnected, or re-authenticated independently.
  • Routing: When your backend triggers an action (send a Slack message, create a HubSpot contact), the action must use the correct tenant's credentials, not a shared pool.
  • Scale: Token refresh, re-authentication prompts, and connection health checks must work reliably across thousands of tenants simultaneously.

Building all of this from scratch — per integration, per provider — is the main reason integration development is consistently underestimated.

The Core Pattern: Identifier-Scoped Credential Storage

The foundation of any multi-tenant integration architecture is a stable, unique identifier per tenant that scopes all credential storage and retrieval.

In viaSocket's model, this is the unique_identifier field in the JWT payload:

const payload = {
  org_id: process.env.VIASOCKET_ORG_ID,
  project_id: process.env.VIASOCKET_PROJECT_ID,
  unique_identifier: tenantId
};

const token = jwt.sign(payload, process.env.VIASOCKET_EMBED_SECRET, {
  algorithm: 'HS256',
  expiresIn: '1h'
});

Every OAuth token viaSocket stores is keyed to this identifier. When your backend requests an action execution for a given unique_identifier, viaSocket retrieves only the credentials belonging to that identifier. Cross-tenant credential access is structurally prevented at the storage layer.

Choosing your identifier: Use your internal tenant or user ID — a stable, immutable string that maps one-to-one to your tenants. Do not use email addresses (they can change), session tokens (they expire), or composite keys that might be reused.

Four Isolation Dimensions

1. Credential Isolation

Each tenant's OAuth tokens are stored under their unique_identifier. Two tenants who both connect Slack get separate token records. Revoking one tenant's connection leaves the other's untouched.

Your responsibility: ensure the unique_identifier in every JWT you sign is correct for the authenticated session. This is a backend concern — the JWT is signed server-side with your embed_secret and delivered to the frontend via a protected API endpoint.

2. Connection State Isolation

Each tenant sees only their own connected apps. The SDK methods are automatically scoped to the unique_identifier from the initialisation token:

// Returns only the apps connected by this tenant
const enabled = await viasocket.user.findEnabled();

// Opens a connection flow scoped to this tenant
await viasocket.connect({ app: 'notion' });

There is no shared connection state across tenants. A tenant who disconnects an app affects only their own record.

3. Action Execution Routing

When your backend triggers an integration action, the unique_identifier in the request body tells viaSocket which tenant's credentials to use:

await fetch(`https://flow.sokt.io/func/${process.env.SCRIPT_ID}`, {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    unique_identifier: tenantId,
    app: 'hubspot',
    action: 'create_contact',
    params: { email: contactEmail, firstname: firstName }
  })
});

The script_id in the URL identifies the workflow. The unique_identifier in the body selects the tenant's credentials. Both are required — neither alone is sufficient to execute a routed action.

4. Re-Authentication Isolation

OAuth tokens expire and get revoked. When a single tenant's connection breaks, only that tenant needs to re-authenticate. Your frontend can check connection health per-tenant and prompt re-authentication selectively, without affecting any other tenant's active connections.

Connection Lifecycle Management

A production multi-tenant integration needs to handle the full connection lifecycle, not just the happy path.

Initial connection: The tenant clicks Connect in your UI, the SDK opens the OAuth flow, viaSocket handles the token exchange, and the token is stored under the tenant's identifier.

Checking connection status: Before executing an action for a tenant, verify the connection exists:

const enabled = await viasocket.user.findEnabled();
const hasSlack = enabled.some(app => app.name === 'slack');

if (!hasSlack) {
  // Prompt the tenant to connect Slack before proceeding
}

Handling disconnection: Tenants can disconnect apps explicitly, or tokens can be revoked by the provider. Your integration logic should handle action failures gracefully and surface re-connection prompts rather than failing silently.

Tenant offboarding: When a tenant leaves your product, revoke and remove their connections. This is both a security practice and a hygiene requirement for maintaining clean credential records.

Scaling Considerations

Don't Store OAuth Tokens Yourself

The most common scaling mistake is duplicating token storage — pulling tokens from a managed OAuth layer and caching them in your own database. This creates two problems: your cache goes stale when tokens refresh, and you are now responsible for the security of credentials you did not need to hold.

If you are using a managed OAuth layer, let it own token storage. Your backend's job is to route requests with the correct unique_identifier, not to hold credentials.

Scope JWT Expiry Tightly

JWTs should have short expiry windows — one hour is a reasonable default. Return a fresh JWT from your backend at the start of each session rather than issuing long-lived tokens. Since the JWT generation is a lightweight signing operation, there is no meaningful performance cost to short expiry.

Keep Script IDs and Secrets in Environment Variables

Your embed_secret (the JWT signing key) and your script_id values are credentials. Store them in environment variables, rotate them if they are exposed, and never include them in client-side code.

AI Agent Integrations

If your product includes AI agent features, the same multi-tenant isolation model applies. When an agent executes a tool call on behalf of a tenant, the action execution must include that tenant's unique_identifier so the correct credentials are used. Do not share a single agent credential set across tenants for actions that operate on tenant-owned data.

Architecture Summary

Concern Responsibility How
Credential storage viaSocket (managed) Keyed to unique_identifier
JWT signing Your backend HS256 with embed_secret; secret never sent to client
Connection UI Your frontend + SDK SDK initialised with per-session JWT
Action execution Your backend POST to flow.sokt.io/func/script_id with unique_identifier
Tenant identifier accuracy Your backend Match JWT unique_identifier to authenticated session
Token refresh viaSocket (managed) Automatic per provider

Related Resources

  • How to Handle OAuth for Multi-Tenant SaaS Integrations with viaSocket
  • Embed Integrations in Your SaaS Product
  • Developer Documentation

posts.title: White-Label MCP Server for SaaS: Ship Native AI Agent Support in Days
posts.description: Launch a white-label MCP server for your SaaS to power native AI agent tool-calling in days. Architecture, deployment model, and how viaSocket fits.
posts.author: Abhijeet Singh
posts.html:
Your users are already using AI assistants. Claude, Cursor, and a growing list of MCP-compatible clients let users connect external tools to their AI environment — and those users will want to connect your product too.

A white-label MCP server lets you meet them there. Instead of waiting for users to ask for an integration, you ship a branded MCP endpoint they paste into their AI client once — and from then on, your product's capabilities are available inside every conversation they have with their AI assistant.

This article covers what a white-label MCP server is, how it works architecturally, what it takes to build versus buy, and how viaSocket's MCP infrastructure fits into a SaaS product.

What a White-Label MCP Server Is

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard that defines how AI clients discover and call external tools. An MCP server exposes a set of named tools — with names, descriptions, and input schemas — that an AI client can discover and invoke.

A white-label MCP server is one that is branded to your SaaS product. Your users see your product name, your domain, and your tool names — not the underlying infrastructure provider's branding. From your user's perspective, they are connecting their AI assistant to your product.

This is distinct from:

  • A generic MCP server (e.g., a public Slack MCP server that anyone can use — not branded to your product)
  • An internal MCP server (used by your own AI agent to call third-party services — not user-facing)
  • An embedded workflow builder (your users configure automations inside your UI — not inside their AI client)

White-label MCP targets a specific interaction: your user is in Claude or Cursor, and they want to act on your product from there.

The Architecture

A white-label MCP deployment for a SaaS product has three layers:

1. The MCP server endpoint

An HTTP(S) endpoint that implements the MCP specification: responds to tool discovery requests with a tool list, and executes tool-call requests. Each SaaS customer (your tenant) gets their own endpoint URL or a URL parameterized by tenant identifier.

2. Tool definitions

Each action your product supports — create project, update record, send notification, fetch report — becomes a named MCP tool with a JSON Schema input definition and a human-readable description. The description matters: the AI model reads it to decide when to use the tool.

3. Auth and execution

When a tool is invoked, the MCP server must authenticate the request (verify it is coming from a legitimate AI client for a legitimate user), then execute the action — calling your product's API, or calling a downstream third-party API on your user's behalf.

Handling auth at scale (per-tenant credentials, OAuth token refresh, secure storage) is the hard part of running an MCP server in production.

Build vs. Buy

Building a white-label MCP server from scratch involves:

  • Implementing the MCP spec (tool discovery, invocation, streaming, error handling)
  • Writing and maintaining tool definitions for every action
  • Building per-tenant auth (OAuth flows, token storage, refresh logic)
  • Hosting, scaling, and monitoring the server
  • Updating tool definitions as your product's API evolves
  • Keeping up with MCP spec updates as the standard matures

For most SaaS teams, this is a meaningful engineering investment — weeks to a first working version, ongoing maintenance thereafter.

The alternative is white-label MCP infrastructure: a platform that provides the server layer, handles the MCP spec implementation, manages per-tenant auth, and exposes your product's actions as tools — so your engineering time goes into defining what your product does, not into protocol plumbing.

How viaSocket's White-Label MCP Works

viaSocket's MCP for SaaS provides white-label MCP server infrastructure for SaaS companies. The key elements:

Branded endpoint: Your users get an MCP endpoint associated with your product. They configure it in their AI client (Claude Desktop, Cursor, or any MCP-compatible client) once.

2,300+ app integrations: The underlying Integration Layer connects to 2,300+ apps. If your product's actions involve reading from or writing to third-party apps (CRMs, project tools, communication platforms), those connections are already built.

Managed OAuth: viaSocket handles the OAuth flows and token storage for the downstream app connections. Your users authenticate once; the infrastructure manages token refresh.

No MCP server to maintain: The MCP spec implementation, hosting, scaling, and spec updates are handled by viaSocket's infrastructure. You ship the integration, not the server.

This fits SaaS builders who want to offer native AI agent support — letting their users call their product from AI clients — without the build time of implementing the MCP protocol themselves.

Who Should Use a White-Label MCP Server

White-label MCP is the right fit when:

  • Your users are already using MCP-compatible AI clients (Claude, Cursor, and a growing list of others)
  • You want your product to be natively accessible from those AI environments
  • You do not want to build and maintain MCP server infrastructure
  • You need per-tenant isolation (each customer gets their own configured endpoint)

It is less relevant if:

  • Your primary need is for your own AI agent to call third-party APIs (that is the use case for Embed Actions for AI)
  • Your users primarily configure integrations through a visual UI inside your product (that is the use case for embedded iPaaS)

These are not mutually exclusive — many SaaS products will eventually want both a white-label MCP server (for users operating from AI clients) and embedded workflow automation (for users configuring integrations inside the product UI).

Competitive Landscape

The white-label MCP space is a growing list of entrants as MCP adoption accelerates. Paragon's ActionKit includes MCP server capabilities positioned primarily at giving your SaaS's own AI agent access to third-party integrations. The distinction worth tracking is whether a solution provides a user-facing branded MCP endpoint (what your users paste into Claude) versus an internal MCP server your AI agent calls — these are architecturally different products serving different interactions.

Evaluate any MCP offering on: per-tenant isolation, who manages the MCP spec implementation and updates, how downstream OAuth is handled, and whether the endpoint is truly white-labeled to your brand.

Deployment in Practice

With viaSocket's white-label MCP, the deployment path for a SaaS team looks like this:

  1. Connect your product's actions to viaSocket's Integration Layer
  2. Configure your white-label MCP endpoint (branding, tool selection, tenant auth)
  3. Provide your users with their personalized MCP endpoint URL
  4. Users paste the URL into Claude Desktop, Cursor, or their preferred MCP client
  5. From that point, the AI client can discover and invoke your product's tools in any conversation

Ongoing: viaSocket handles MCP spec compliance, server uptime, and OAuth token management. You update tool definitions when your product's capabilities change.

Implementation Details

For technical details on the viaSocket Integration Layer, SDK, and auth patterns, see the Developers Docs. The SDK supports Node 20+, Bun, Deno, and edge runtimes, with zero dependencies and MIT licensing.

For the full feature set of the Integration Layer that backs the MCP server, see Integration Layer features.

FAQ

What AI clients can connect to a white-label MCP server?

Any AI client that has implemented the MCP client specification. This currently includes Claude Desktop, Cursor, and a growing list of other AI development environments and assistants. The list is expanding as MCP adoption grows.

Do my users need to configure anything?

Users paste their personalized MCP endpoint URL into their AI client's MCP server settings once. After that, the AI client handles discovery and invocation automatically.

How is per-tenant isolation handled?

Each of your customers (tenants) gets their own configured endpoint or parameterized URL. Their credentials and OAuth tokens are stored and managed separately. One tenant's actions cannot access another tenant's data.

What happens when the MCP spec is updated?

With viaSocket's infrastructure, MCP spec updates are handled by the platform — you do not need to update your implementation when the protocol evolves.

How does this differ from building our own MCP server?

Building your own requires implementing the MCP spec, managing per-tenant OAuth, hosting and scaling the server, and keeping up with spec changes. White-label MCP infrastructure handles all of that so your team focuses on defining your product's tools, not on protocol plumbing.

Can we use this alongside an embedded workflow builder?

Yes. White-label MCP (users calling your product from their AI client) and embedded iPaaS (users configuring workflows inside your product UI) serve different user interactions and coexist well in a complete integration strategy.

posts.title: API Rate Limiting for Multi-Tenant Integrations
posts.description: In a multi-tenant product, rate limiting stops being "catch the 429 and back off" and becomes a resource-allocation problem. How to track and enforce limits per tenant, not just per provider.
posts.author: Abhijeet Singh
posts.html:
Every third-party API you integrate with enforces some kind of rate limit, and almost every guide on handling them assumes you're a single consumer talking to a single API on behalf of yourself. That assumption breaks the moment your product has more than one customer.

If you're building integrations into a multi-tenant SaaS product — where Customer A and Customer B both connect their own Salesforce, HubSpot, or Slack account through your app — rate limiting stops being "catch the 429 and back off" and becomes a resource-allocation problem: whose requests get to run, in what order, when the shared budget is tight. Get this wrong, and the usual failure mode isn't a crash. It's one customer's bulk import quietly starving every other customer's sync for the next twenty minutes.

This is a practical guide to that specific problem: tracking and enforcing rate limits per tenant, not just per provider, inside an integration layer that serves many customers at once.

Why single-tenant rate-limit advice doesn't transfer

The standard rate-limit playbook is well documented elsewhere: read Retry-After, back off exponentially with jitter, use a token bucket, add a circuit breaker. All of that is still necessary. None of it answers the question that actually matters in a multi-tenant system: whose token bucket is it?

Two patterns collide here, and most teams only notice the collision in production:

  • Provider-level limits are usually set per API key, per OAuth app, or per account — not per end user of your product. If ten of your customers connect to Salesforce through the same connected app, Salesforce may be rate-limiting your app's traffic as a whole, not each customer individually.

  • Tenant-level fairness is what your customers actually expect. Customer A importing 50,000 contacts should not cause Customer B's single webhook-triggered sync to queue for ten minutes behind it.

A rate limiter built for a single consumer optimizes for "stay under the ceiling." A rate limiter built for a multi-tenant integration layer has to optimize for "stay under the ceiling and divide what's left fairly" — and those two goals require different data structures, not just a bigger bucket.

The shared-quota problem, concretely

Say your product integrates with a CRM that allows 1,000 requests per minute per connected app, and 40 of your customers have connected their own accounts of that CRM through the same OAuth app registration. Three things can go wrong, and they compound:

  1. Noisy neighbor. One customer runs a bulk operation — a CSV import, a full historical backfill — and consumes most of the 1,000-request budget for that minute. Every other customer sharing the same app registration gets throttled, even though their own usage is tiny.

  2. Silent unfairness. Without per-tenant tracking, you can't even tell which customer caused the throttling after the fact. Your support team sees "sync is slow" tickets from customers who did nothing wrong, with no data to point at the actual cause.

  3. Retry amplification. If every tenant's sync worker independently implements its own retry-with-backoff against the same shared 429, you get a thundering herd within your own system — forty workers all backing off and retrying against a limit none of them individually caused.

The fix isn't a smarter backoff curve. It's making the rate limiter tenant-aware before the request is sent, not just reactive after a 429 comes back.

Designing a tenant-aware rate limiter

A multi-tenant integration layer needs two layers of budget, tracked separately, and reconciled on every outbound call:

Layer 1 — the provider budget. The actual ceiling the third-party API enforces (requests per second/minute/day, concurrent connections, or a leaky/token-bucket model specific to that provider). This is shared across every tenant hitting that provider through the same credentials.

Layer 2 — the per-tenant allocation. A slice of the provider budget assigned to each connected tenant, so one customer's burst can't silently consume another's share.

A simple and effective allocation model is a weighted token bucket per (tenant, provider connection) pair, refilled from a shared pool:

shared_pool.capacity = provider_limit_per_window
shared_pool.refill_rate = provider_limit_per_window / window_seconds

per_tenant_bucket[tenant_id].capacity = min(
  fair_share * burst_multiplier,
  shared_pool.capacity
)

Where fair_share is shared_pool.capacity / active_tenant_count, recalculated periodically rather than per request. burst_multiplier (typically 2–4x) lets a quiet tenant use more than their strict equal share when the pool isn't contended, without ever exceeding the shared ceiling. Before any request goes out: acquire a token from both the tenant's bucket and the shared pool. If either is empty, the request queues — against that tenant's own queue, not a global one, so one tenant's backlog doesn't block another's dequeue order.

This is the same acquire-before-send discipline covered in the multi-tenant integration architecture pattern for delivery and credentials generally: rate-limit budgets are a fourth isolation dimension alongside credentials, routing, and observability, and they need the same per-connection accounting the others get.

Separate credentials beat shared credentials, where the provider allows it

The cleanest fix to the noisy-neighbor problem is structural, not algorithmic: get each tenant their own API credentials instead of routing all tenants through one shared OAuth app or API key.

Some providers make this easy — Shopify, for example, issues rate limits per shop (effectively per tenant) rather than per app, so a well-architected integration naturally gets tenant isolation for free. Others don't: a single Slack app's rate limits are shared across every workspace it's installed in unless you specifically request enterprise-grid-level isolation.

Where per-tenant credentials are available, use them, even though it means more OAuth flows and more token lifecycle management per connection. Where they're not, the shared-pool-plus-fair-share model above is the next best thing, and it's worth building deliberately rather than discovering you need it after your first large customer starves your smaller ones.

Prioritizing requests, not just rate-limiting them

Not all API calls a tenant generates are equal, and a rate limiter that treats a user-triggered action (someone clicking "sync now" and waiting) the same as a background batch job (a nightly full resync) will make the wrong tradeoff under pressure.

A practical priority scheme:

Priority Example Behavior under contention
Interactive User clicks a button, expects a result in seconds Reserve a small always-available slice of the tenant's bucket; never queued behind batch work
Event-driven Webhook-triggered single-record sync Normal queue, short timeout, fail fast and retry later rather than blocking
Batch/background Historical import, nightly resync Lowest priority, explicitly throttled to leave headroom, allowed to run over a longer window

Implementing this doesn't require a sophisticated scheduler — a small number of separate queues per tenant, drained in priority order, with the interactive queue getting first access to that tenant's token bucket, gets most of the benefit. The expensive part is remembering to classify every new integration's calls into one of these buckets at write time, not retrofitting it later once a batch job has already degraded someone's interactive experience.

What this looks like when a limit is actually hit

Tenant-aware allocation reduces how often you hit a provider's ceiling, but it doesn't eliminate 429s — a tenant can still legitimately need more throughput than their fair share allows during a real burst. When that happens, the same reactive patterns from single-tenant rate limiting still apply, scoped per tenant:

  • Respect Retry-After when the provider sends it; fall back to jittered exponential backoff when it doesn't.

  • Keep backoff state per tenant, not global — a backoff triggered by Tenant A's traffic shouldn't throttle Tenant B's independent requests against the same provider.

  • Distinguish a rate limit (wait and retry) from a quota exhaustion (daily/monthly cap — stop and alert, since retrying won't help until the window resets).

  • Feed 429 frequency per tenant into monitoring, not just a global error rate — a single tenant repeatedly tripping limits is a different problem (undersized allocation, or a misbehaving sync job) than broad provider-wide throttling.

This reliability layer sits next to the work covered in our guide to webhook retries and idempotency — that piece covers the inbound side (a provider delivering events to you reliably), while rate limiting covers the outbound side (your system calling a provider without overwhelming its ceiling or starving other tenants). Both ultimately rely on the same per-tenant isolation discipline, and both sit downstream of a connection that was authenticated correctly in the first place — see how OAuth integrations are typically built for the layer underneath both.

Build vs. buy, for this specific piece

Tenant-aware rate limiting is one of those features that's straightforward to describe and genuinely tedious to build correctly: a shared-pool token bucket, per-tenant queues, priority classification, backoff state tracked per connection, and monitoring that can answer "which tenant caused this" — all of it has to be re-derived for every provider you add, because every provider's actual limit shape (requests per second vs. concurrent connections vs. a daily quota) is different.

It's also the kind of infrastructure that only becomes visible as a gap once you have enough tenants for the shared-quota math to matter — which is exactly when it's most expensive to retrofit, because by then real customers are the ones queued behind someone else's import job.

This is part of what an embedded integration layer like viaSocket is built to absorb: per-connection rate-limit tracking, retry and backoff handled centrally, and tenant isolation that extends to API throughput, not just credentials and data — so a product team adding a new integration inherits fair, tenant-aware request handling instead of rebuilding the allocation logic for every provider they connect to.

Key takeaways

  • Standard rate-limit advice (backoff, jitter, token buckets) assumes a single consumer; multi-tenant products need a second layer that allocates a shared provider quota fairly across tenants.

  • Track two budgets per request: the provider's actual limit, and each tenant's fair share of it — enforced with a weighted token bucket refilled from a shared pool.

  • Use separate API credentials per tenant where the provider supports it; it removes the noisy-neighbor problem structurally instead of managing around it.

  • Classify requests by priority (interactive, event-driven, batch) and queue per tenant, so one customer's bulk job never blocks another's real-time action.

  • Keep backoff and 429 monitoring scoped per tenant — a single customer repeatedly tripping limits is a different incident than provider-wide throttling.

FAQs

Does every API provider rate-limit per app or per account?

It varies. Some (like Shopify) rate-limit per shop/tenant natively, which gives you isolation for free. Many others (common with Slack, many CRMs under a single OAuth app) rate-limit the app as a whole, meaning every tenant connected through that app shares one ceiling unless you request separate credentials per tenant.

Is a bigger token bucket the fix for noisy-neighbor throttling?

No — a bigger shared bucket just delays the problem; it doesn't allocate it fairly. The fix is a second, per-tenant bucket layered on top of the shared provider bucket, so no single tenant can consume more than their allotted share even when the shared bucket has room.

Should background jobs and user-facing requests share the same rate limit queue?

No. Give interactive, user-triggered requests priority access to a tenant's budget, and run batch or background syncs in a lower-priority queue with their own throttling, so a nightly resync never makes a customer wait on a button click.

What's the difference between hitting a rate limit and hitting a quota?

A rate limit is a per-second/minute/hour ceiling that resets quickly — wait and retry. A quota is a longer window (daily/monthly) that doesn't reset until the period ends — retrying aggressively won't help, and the better response is to alert and pause until the quota resets or is increased.
